entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 4 Zec 4:1-14 . Fifth Vision. The golden candlestick and the two olive trees. The temple shall be completed by the aid of God's Spirit. 1. waked me-- The prophet was lying in a state of ecstatic slumber with astonishment at the previous vision. "Came again, and waked me," does not imply that the angel had departed and now returned, but is an idiom for "waked me again."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13054"/><div sID="gen24523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13054"/><hi type="bold">2. candlestick--</hi>symbolizing the Jewish theocracy; and ultimately, the Church of which the Jewish portion is to be the head: the light-bearer (so the original is of "lights," <reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">Mt 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.15">Php 2:15</reference>) to the world.<div eID="gen24523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... gold--</hi>all pure in doctrine and practice, precious and indestructible; such is the true ideal of the Church; such she shall be (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>).<div eID="gen24524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bowl upon the top--</hi>In the candlestick of the tabernacle the plural is used, bowls (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.31">Ex 25:31</reference>). The Hebrew implies that it was the fountain of supply of oil to the lamps. Christ at the head ("on the top") of the Church is the true fountain, of whose fulness of the Spirit all we receive grace (<reference osisRef="John.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>).<div eID="gen24525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his seven lamps--</hi>united in one stem; so in <reference osisRef="Exod.25.32">Ex 25:32</reference>. But in <reference osisRef="Rev.1.12">Re 1:12</reference> the seven candlesticks are separate. The Gentile churches will not realize their unity till the Jewish Church as the stem unites all the lamps in one candlestick (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.16-Rom.11.24">Ro 11:16-24</reference>). The "seven lamps," in <reference osisRef="Rev.4.5">Re 4:5</reference>, are the "seven Spirits of God."<div eID="gen24526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven pipes--</hi>feeding tubes, seven apiece from the "bowl" to each lamp (see Margin) [Maurer and Calvin]; literally, "seven and seven": forty-nine in all. The greater the number of oil-feeding pipes, the brighter the light of the lamps. The explanation in <reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zec 4:6</reference> is, that man's power by itself can neither retard nor advance God's work, that the real motive-power is God's Spirit. The seven times seven imply the manifold modes by which the Spirit's grace is imparted to the Church in her manifold work of enlightening the world. <div eID="gen24527" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13058"/><div sID="gen24533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13058"/><hi type="bold">6. Not by might ... but by my Spirit--</hi>As the lamps burned continually, supplied with oil from a source (the living olive trees) which man did not make, so Zerubbabel need not be disheartened because of his weakness; for as the work is one to be effected by the living Spirit (compare <reference osisRef="Hag.2.5">Hag 2:5</reference>) of God, man's weakness is no obstacle, for God's might will perfect strength out of weakness (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.7">Ho 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">2Co 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.34">He 11:34</reference>). "Might and power" express human strength of every description, physical, mental, moral. Or, "might" is the strength of many (an "army," literally); "power," that of one man [Pembellus]. God can save, "whether with many, or with them that have no power" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.11">2Ch 14:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1Sa 14:6</reference>). So in the conversion of sinners (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1Co 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2Co 10:4</reference>). "Zerubbabel" is addressed as the chief civil authority in directing the work. <div eID="gen24533" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13059"/><div sID="gen24534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13059"/>7. All mountain-like obstacles (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.4">Is 40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.11">49:11</reference>) in Zerubbabel's way shall be removed, so that the crowning top-stone shall be put on, and the completion of the work be acknowledged as wholly of "grace." Antitypically, the antichristian last foe of Israel, the obstacle preventing her establishment in Palestine, about to be crushed before Messiah, is probably meant (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.25">Jr 51:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>, 44; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mt 21:44</reference>).<div eID="gen24534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring forth the head-stone--</hi>Primarily, bring it forth from the place where it was chiselled and give it to the workmen to put on the top of the building. It was customary for chief magistrates to lay the foundation, and also the crowning top-stone (compare <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.10">Ezr 3:10</reference>). Antitypically, the reference is to the time when the full number of the spiritual Church shall be completed, and also when "all Israel shall be saved" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">He 11:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">12:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.4-Rev.7.9">Re 7:4-9</reference>).<div eID="gen24535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Grace, grace--</hi>The repetition expresses, Grace from first to last (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Is 26:3</reference>, Margin). Thus the Jews are urged to pray perseveringly and earnestly that the same grace which completed it may always preserve it. "Shoutings" of acclamation accompanied the foundation of the literal temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.11">Ezr 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.13">13</reference>). So shoutings of "Hosanna" greeted the Saviour in entering Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">Mt 21:9</reference>), when about to complete the purchase of salvation by His death: His Body being the second temple, or place of God's inhabitation (<reference osisRef="John.2.20">Joh 2:20</reference>, 21). So when the full number of the saints and of Israel is complete, and God shall say, "It is done," then again shall "a great voice of much people in heaven" attribute all to the "grace" of God, saying, "Alleluia! Salvation, and glory, and honor, and power, unto the Lord our God" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.1">Re 19:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.6">6</reference>). <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference> regards Him as "the head-stone of the corner," that is, the foundation-stone. Compare the angels acclamations at His birth, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Lu 2:14</reference>. Here it is the top-stone. Messiah is not only the "Author," but also the Finisher (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">He 12:2</reference>). "Grace" is ascribed "unto it," that is, the stone, Messiah. Hence the benediction begins, "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.14">2Co 13:14</reference>). <div eID="gen24536" type="x-p"/>

Zerubbabel ... shall ... finish it--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.15">Ezr 6:15</reference>) in the sixth year of Darius' reign.<div eID="gen24537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord ... sent me unto you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.2.9">Zec 2:9</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13061"/><div sID="gen24539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13061"/><hi type="bold">10. who ... despised ... small things--</hi>He reproves their ungrateful unbelief, which they felt because of the humble beginning, compared with the greatness of the undertaking; and encourages them with the assurance that their progress in the work, though small, was an earnest of great and final success, because Jehovah's eye is upon Zerubbabel and the work, to support Him with His favor. Contrast, "great is the day of Jezreel" (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Ho 1:11</reference>) with "the day of small things" here.<div eID="gen24539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall rejoice ... with those seven; they are the eyes of the Lord--</hi>rather, "they, even those seven eyes of the Lord (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference>), which ... shall rejoice and see (that is, rejoicingly see) the plummet (literally, the 'stone of tin') in the hand of Zerubbabel" [Moore]; the plummet in his hand indicating that the work is going forward to its completion. The Hebrew punctuation, however, favors English Version, of which the sense is, They who incredulously "despised" such "small" beginnings of the work as are made now, shall rejoicingly see its going on to completion under Zerubbabel, "with (the aid of) those seven," namely, the "seven eyes upon one stone" (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference>): which are explained, "They are the eyes of the Lord which," &c. [Pembellus]. So differently do men and Jehovah regard the "small" beginnings of God's work (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezr 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hag.2.3">Hag 2:3</reference>). Men "despised" the work in its early stage: God rejoicingly regards it, and shall continue to do so.<div eID="gen24540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">run to and fro, &c.--</hi>Nothing in the whole earth escapes the eye of Jehovah, so that He can ward off all danger from His people, come from what quarter it may, in prosecuting His work (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">Pr 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.9">1Co 16:9</reference>). <div eID="gen24541" type="x-p"/>

Contrast, "great is the day of Jezreel" ( Ho 1:11 ) with "the day of small things" here. they shall rejoice ... with those seven; they are the eyes of the Lord-- rather, "they, even those seven eyes of the Lord (compare Zec 3:9 ), which ... shall rejoice and see (that is, rejoicingly see) the plummet (literally, the 'stone of tin') in the hand of Zerubbabel" [Moore]; the plummet in his hand indicating that the work is going forward to its completion. The Hebrew punctuation, however, favors English Version, of which the sense is, They who incredulously "despised" such "small" beginnings of the work as are made now, shall rejoicingly see its going on to completion under Zerubbabel, "with (the aid of) those seven," namely, the "seven eyes upon one stone" ( Zec 3:9 ): which are explained, "They are the eyes of the Lord which," &c. [Pembellus]. So differently do men and Jehovah regard the "small" beginnings of God's work ( Ezr 3:12 ; Hag 2:3 ).
